prize_parts.citation: For the development of massively parallel DNA sequencing by synthesis, using reversibly terminated fluorescent nucleotides on clustered single molecules
For the development of base editing, the programmable chemical conversion of single DNA bases without double-strand cleavage

statement.case_for: I have moved my first part from B053 to B011. The chair asked for second-choice configurations that could draw wider support, and after reading all eight files B011 is the only part that two members prefer and several others describe as the cleanest attribution on the shortlist. It also meets my own test of molecule-making. The reversible terminator with a cleavable fluorophore and a removable 3'-blocking group is a designed nucleotide, a synthetic-chemistry solution to a stepwise-reaction problem, and the chemistry was then confirmed for fifteen years by every group that built on it. I would word the citation around the terminator chemistry on clustered single molecules so that it rewards the invention, not the field or the platform. Base editing stays as the second part, credited to Liu alone, because Liu's group made both the cytosine and adenine editors, and the adenine editor, which needed evolved TadA, has no counterpart elsewhere. This is deaminase chemistry applied to DNA, and it has reached patients. The two parts are distinct achievements, they share a theme of chemistry on nucleic acids without being one field, and the configuration uses exactly three people (Balasubramanian, Klenerman, Liu).
statement.case_against: A sceptic can read B011 as a platform or medicine achievement, and Rothberg's 454 pyrosequencing, Mayer's clustering and Ju's terminator work are left out; I cannot settle those priority questions from recollection and would want the expert reports to do so. Base editing follows the 2020 CRISPR prize within six years, the clinical record is short, and the deaminase is a natural enzyme repurposed by protein engineering, so the chemical novelty is real but less than in a new bond-forming reaction. Two nucleic-acid-centred parts could look like a biology-leaning prize, and I give up B053, which I still consider the clearest general method on the list, because only two members ranked it and the 2010 prize colours how it is read.

responses.point: Aqvist prefers Balasubramanian and Klenerman alone for sequencing by synthesis, excludes 454 pyrosequencing from the core credit, and lists B012 as an alternative.
responses.response: I now agree with him and adopt B011 as my first part. His argument that the reversible-terminator chemistry is the decisive invention is the one a synthetic chemist should find persuasive, and 454 is chemically a different method. I would not add Mayer or Ju without a clear finding from the expert reports on who made the terminator and clustering steps. Where I differ is that I would pair it with Liu instead of leaving it alone, since a single-part prize would drop a mature candidate that several of us already rank. I would ask him whether he could accept B012 as a second part, given that it was already on his alternatives list.

responses.point: Linke pairs B011 with a nanopore part credited to Bayley alone and lists B034 and B012 as alternatives, while himself raising the attribution problem for B001.
responses.response: We agree on B011, so I would ask him to consider B012 in place of B001. The chair's own summary shows the obstacles for nanopores: five claimants, Branton deceased, and Bayley's status unverified, so naming one person leaves out Deamer and Akeson, who did the strand-level discrimination and enzyme ratcheting. B012 is one of his listed alternatives and gives a clean one-name credit. His physical argument for nanopores is elegant, but I cannot build a prize on it until the credit can be defended, and unlike him I would not stack two sequencing methods in one prize.

responses.point: Aili prefers B034 with Crews and Deshaies plus B012 with Liu alone, and says base editing is a designable chemical conversion.
responses.response: I take the point that base editing is chemistry that can be designed: a deaminase fused to a Cas9 nickase converts one base to another on a defined position. This is why I keep Liu as the second part. We agree on Liu alone and on rejecting Kondo and Nishida, since Target-AID is a parallel cytidine editor and the adenine editor has no counterpart. We differ on the first part. I rank B034 as an alternative, not preferred, because no PROTAC drug is approved and the credit is split between PROTACs and cereblon glues. If the committee wants a degrader prize, I would support a Crews and Deshaies citation worded narrowly on the bifunctional concept.

responses.point: Chabes prefers B034 with Crews, Deshaies and Handa, and treats the cereblon glue arm as the strongest evidence of maturity.
responses.response: The glue arm is a fair point on maturity, because lenalidomide and pomalidomide have a long patient record that explains how the drugs work. My concern is the one I raised in round one: one citation that spans PROTACs and cereblon would credit two discoveries with three names, leaving out Ciulli, Sakamoto, Kim, Gray and Ito. That is difficult for any trio to defend and would put four of the eight names outside the prize in a field still moving fast. He also asks how much of B011 is chemistry; I believe the terminator nucleotide is clearly chemistry, which is why the citation must name it.

responses.point: Zou prefers Corma, Davis and Zones for molecular-sieve catalysts and flags that the 2025 MOF prize is a timing problem for porous materials.
responses.response: I see the structure-determines-function case, and I rank it near the clean attributions on the list. I agree the MOF prize creates an optics problem, as I said about B053 and the 2010 prize. I would apply the same standard to both: when the area has just been honoured, a new prize needs a distinct mechanism and a distinct group of people. For zeolites I am not convinced it passes that test this year, and the three-person cut leaves out Jihong Yu and Tsapatsis. I appreciate her offer to recuse from B051, and I think it is the right instinct.

uncertainties: Whether the expert reports establish who made the reversible terminator and clustering steps, and whether Mayer, Ju or Rothberg would have to be credited alongside Balasubramanian and Klenerman.
Whether the committee treats sequencing by synthesis as chemistry or as a platform achievement, which depends on the citation wording and could cost votes.
Whether base editing is judged distinct enough in principle from the 2020 CRISPR prize, and whether its short clinical record is enough to decide against it.
Whether this pairing, with one supporter of each part in the first round, can reach five votes, given the dispersion the chair documented.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict with any shortlisted candidate. I have no tie to Balasubramanian, Klenerman, Liu, Buchwald or Hartwig, and my Masamune postdoctoral background is not a connection to any of them. I note shared Lund affiliation with Linke and Sparr, who each prefer other parts, and I do not treat it as a conflict.
